write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/ssr-ring. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/ssr-ring to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/ssr-ring; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/ssr-ring plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/ssr-ring that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

description:

title: SSR refuses an explicit :payload [] as a missing policy, so 'ship nothing' is taught as the most permissive policy; accept an empty allowlist
description:
An explicit, empty `:payload []` is refused as a missing policy. So the documented way to ship "nothing" is the most permissive policy there is, and that policy starts shipping everything as soon as server code fills app-db.

## Where

`valid-allowlist?` in `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/payload_policy.cljc` requires `(seq x)`, so `:payload []` lands in `:rf.error/ssr-missing-payload-policy`.

The namespace docstring calls zero keys "almost certainly a programmer error". It tells callers to use `:payload :rf.ssr.payload/whole-app-db` "against an empty `app-db`" instead. A computed allowlist that is legitimately empty (`(filterv …)`) also fails at boot.

Two texts state the same rule:
- Spec 011 §`:rf/app-db` projection: "An empty `:payload` (`[]` / `'()`) is treated as no-allowlist".
- `render_state.cljc` `allowlist-shape-problem` rejects an empty slot the same way ("is empty — an allowlist that names nothing is no allowlist").

## Change

An empty sequential becomes a valid allowlist that projects `{}`, for both `:payload` and `:render-state` slots.

Preserve:
- an absent or nil `:payload` still raises the missing-policy error;
- sets, non-keyword entries and unknown keywords keep their errors.

Add no new policy keyword and no warning.

## Files

- `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/{payload_policy,render_state}.cljc` and their `_cljs_test.cljc` files.
- `spec/011-SSR.md`. This is the one `i/crlf` file in the repo: edit it with the Edit/Write tools and check CR == CRLF with Python afterwards.
- `docs/ssr/concepts.md` (~L243, ~L614).

No hot-zone file. rf2-e2x5y also edits `spec/011-SSR.md`, so sequence the two.

Supporting detail, local to this machine only: `C:\Users\miket\code\re-frame2\ai\findings\advisarial-review\sol-history\2026-10-15-low-hanging-fruit\before\27-ssr-rendering.md` §3 and `...\28-ssr-hydration-egress.md` §3.
acceptance_criteria:
1. `{:payload []}` validates. With app-db populated, the payload carries `:rf/app-db {}`.
2. An absent or nil `:payload` still throws the missing-policy error.
3. An empty `:render-state` slot projects that partition as `{}`.
4. Spec 011, `docs/ssr/concepts.md` and the former rejection tests state the new rule, and `spec/011-SSR.md` keeps its CRLF line endings.

title: Unit-test pruning: http
description:
Apply Mike's pruning prompt to implementation/http/test recursively in an isolated worker worktree. This is a distinct cluster in rf2-0wcq5. Push a test-only draft PR, babysit all checks until green, then mark ready; do not merge. Report no-op with evidence instead of manufacturing changes.

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/http/test. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/http/test. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/http/test to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/http/test; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/http/test plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/http/test that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: The CLJS test-quiet harness passes RF2_VERBOSE_TESTS to its child runs, so a verbose test:cljs fails the quiet-output test
description:
`implementation/test-quiet/test/re_frame/test_quiet_shadow_node_cljs_test.cljs` spawns child shadow-node runs without stripping `RF2_VERBOSE_TESTS` from their environment. Since PR #11276 (rf2-9sf6u) makes the runners print a banner per namespace under that flag, `RF2_VERBOSE_TESTS=1 npm run test:cljs` would fail `real-shadow-node-green-run-is-quiet`, which expects summary-only output. Default CI does not set the flag, so CI is unaffected. Found by the rf2-9sf6u worker on 2026-10-15. It was left alone because a fix could not be proved without the shadow-cljs lane.

Fix: strip `RF2_VERBOSE_TESTS` from the child environment in that harness, the same way #11276 does for the JVM harness in test_quiet_runner_contract_test.clj. Prove it: with `RF2_VERBOSE_TESTS=1` set in the outer shell, `npm run test:cljs` (or the build that runs that namespace) fails before and passes after. Needs a shadow-cljs lane grant. Test-only, one file, no hot-zone file.
notes:

title: Two more queued-GC-check interleavings collect early: an adopt-owner attach that re-arms nothing, and a settle re-arm during an in-flight refetch
description:
PR #11299 (rf2-j3k7z) closes the measured queued-GC-check race with an arm-time owner flag.
- `schedule!` records whether the entry had an active owner when its GC timer armed.
- The `gc-fired` payload carries `:armed-while-owned? true`.
- A flagged check that finds the entry owner-free skips as `:superseded`.

The rf2-j3k7z worker found two more interleavings of the same class that the flag does not cover. Each lets a queued check from a superseded window collect an entry early:

1. A timer armed while the entry was owner-free. Its check queues behind the final release AND behind an owner attach that re-arms nothing. `adopt-owner` is such an attach; an attach through a fresh-skip ensure does re-arm while owned, so that path is already covered.
2. An ownerless entry's timer fires while a refetch is in flight. Its check queues behind the success reply, the settle re-arms, and the check then collects the entry immediately.

Suggested shape (not a ruling): one window generation stored ON THE ENTRY in runtime-db.
- Bump it whenever a GC window is (re-)armed.
- Carry it on `gc-fired`.
- Treat a check whose generation is not the entry's current one as superseded.

This keeps the handler a pure function of payload plus runtime-db, so replay stays deterministic. That was the worker's reason to reject a host timer-table token. It would cover both interleavings and could replace the arm-time flag. Preserve:
- stale/poll timers;
- ownerless prefetch collection;
- `:never`;
- server gating;
- #11280's rule that an owned skip arms nothing and an in-flight skip re-arms.

Acceptance: a queued-delivery regression for each interleaving, red on trunk and green with the fix. Use held router drains, as in resources_gc_queued_check_cljs_test.cljc.

Fenced on rf2-j3k7z (PR #11299) merging. Files: implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/timers.cljc and the GC paths of events.cljc, plus a new resources test namespace.
notes:
== IMPLEMENTED (PR #11310, branch worker/resource-gc-window, 2026-10-16) ==
Mechanism: one GC window generation on the entry, `:gc-window` (runtime-db). It replaces #11299's `:armed-while-owned?` flag.
- events.cljc `open-gc-window` bumps it. It runs for every read-path event that arms a GC timer: the scalar success settle, the first-load error and abort settles, the page success settle, the page first-load error and abort settles, the fresh-skip owner revival, the final owner release, and the in-flight GC skip. It bumps only when a timer really arms: a positive delay on a client frame. A server frame never bumps, so the SSR wire is unchanged.
- timers/schedule! reads the entry's `:gc-window` as a GC timer arms. The value replaces entry-owned? and rides the gc-fired payload as `:gc-window`.
- gc-fired-handler marks a check `:superseded` when its window is older than the entry's. A superseded check collects nothing and arms nothing. A check with no window (a direct dispatch) is judged current, so the existing direct-dispatch tests are unchanged.
Tip reproductions (b40493b655, queued delivery with held drains), both in resources_gc_queued_check_cljs_test.cljc:
1. Ownerless settle at t=0, adopt-owner attach, release queued at t=900, timer fires at t=1000. FIFO is [release-owner, gc-fired], and the entry was collected at t=1000.
2. Ownerless settle at t=0, ownerless refetch at t=500, success reply queued at t=900, timer fires at t=1000. FIFO is [succeeded, gc-fired], and the entry was collected right after the re-arming settle.
On tip the namespace exited 1 with 4 failures. With the fix it exits 0 with 4 tests and 14 assertions. A sabotage plant of `superseded? false` exited 1 with 6 failures, two in each of the three queued-check tests, #11299's included.
The full resources JVM lane exits 0 both times: 539 tests and 1537 assertions on tip, 541 tests and 1545 assertions with the change, a delta of +2 tests and +8 assertions as predicted.
Residual in the same race class, outside this bead's files: mutation_events.cljc arms GC for populated or patched keys without opening a window. An ownerless entry's check queued behind such a mutation settle can still collect early, no worse than before. Fixing it takes one open-gc-window-style bump there. The hydration re-arm in ssr.cljc needs no window.
Spec 016 was not edited. No sentence describes the window wrongly. The §Status semantics entry block does not list `:gc-window`.
close_reason: Merged in PR #11310, as one mechanism. The entry now has a :gc-window generation, bumped by open-gc-window only when a GC timer really arms (positive delay, client frame). That happens in the settle handlers, the fresh-skip owner revival, the final owner release and the in-flight GC skip. timers/schedule! stamps the window, and gc-fired-handler treats an older window as :superseded: it collects nothing and arms nothing. A check carrying no window counts as current. This replaces #11299's :armed-while-owned? flag. Both interleavings were reproduced on tip with queued delivery and held drains: adopt-owner FIFO [release-owner, gc-fired], and refetch-settle FIFO [succeeded, gc-fired]. Tip with tests only: exit 1, 4 failures. With the fix: exit 0, 4 tests / 14 assertions. Planting superseded?=false gave exit 1 with 6 failures, so #11299's case now rides on the window. Resources JVM lane went from 539/1537 to 541/1545, exit 0, and clj-kondo was clean. Merge check: rollup 88 (58 pass, 30 skip, 0 bad), 0 live runs, 0 workflow drift. title: Unit-test pruning: event-conformance
description:
Apply the exact requested pruning prompt recursively to implementation/event-conformance/test. This is a distinct worker cluster under rf2-0wcq5. Production code remains unchanged except temporary hash-verified fault plants. Push a draft test-only PR, babysit all latest-head checks to green, then mark ready. A measured no-op or unexecuted-file report is valid; do not manufacture changes.

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/event-conformance/test. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/event-conformance/test. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/event-conformance/test to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/event-conformance/test; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/event-conformance/test plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/event-conformance/test that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: ssr-node: the render module returns its body markup as a string; delete emit, chunk frames and ?stream=1
description:
## Ruling The `ssr-node` render module returns its body markup as a string: `render(call) -> string | Promise`. The `emit` callback, chunk frames, the `renderFrames` generator, the HTTP `?stream=1` mode, surrogate hold-back, `afterChunks` / torn responses, the `x-rf-ssr-chunks` header and the exact-`undefined` return rule all go. A non-string (or a promise that does not resolve to a string) is refused with the existing closed `:rf.ssr-node/render-threw` wording. With streaming SSR parked, "streaming stays behind the server abstraction" no longer binds the module contract; a future streaming design adds a stream-returning form behind the same `:renderer` seam, additively, with its own flow-control and cancellation design. The pre-registered latency envelope stays as a test. Decided 2026-10-16: Mike directed that every dossier recommendation an independent Codex review agreed with be actioned: > review all decisions. They now have a "Codex Recomendation" section. Where the original recomendation matches the Code Recomendation, create a bead to action the decision. And then remove the file. Leave behind cases where the two differ materially. Decisive facts, at trunk 89517e8f54: 1. Nothing consumes the stream. The JVM adapter POSTs to `/render`, never `?stream=1` (`implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/node.clj:271`), and returns the whole buffered body as `{:body-html (str body) :render-hash nil}` (`node.clj:437`). Spec 011 specifies one whole-page response (`spec/011-SSR.md:1404`), and streaming SSR was parked by rf2-mn2ht.31 (2026-10-10). Fresco's `render-body` (`implementation/fresco/src/re_frame/fresco/server.cljs:470`) calls React's `renderToString` and returns that string (`server.cljs:543-552`), and its namespace doc says streaming is "absent, not deferred" (`server.cljs:36-38`). 2. The exact-`undefined` rule is a trap. Any return other than `undefined`, `null` included, is refused with `MODULE_RETURN_REFUSAL` (`implementation/ssr-node/src/protocol.cjs:207-212`, enforced at `implementation/ssr-node/src/worker.cjs:244-257`), so every CLJS module must end in `js/undefined` because `nil` compiles to `null` (`docs/ssr/concepts.md:863-866`). 3. The streaming shape is unfinished: an unbounded `pendingFrames` queue (`implementation/ssr-node/src/service.cjs:114`), an unchecked `res.write` result (`implementation/ssr-node/src/http.cjs:215`), and no producer acknowledgement or cancellation when iteration is abandoned. Rejected options: - **B-emit (keep as is):** about 300 source lines of streaming lifecycle with no producer and no consumer, plus the `js/undefined` trap. - **B-emit-lenient (keep `emit`, accept and ignore any return):** fixes the `nil` trap but keeps the unfinished streaming machinery. - **Switching to `renderToStaticMarkup`:** not hydratable. The string contract preserves React's `renderToString` choice; it does not justify changing it. Supersedes: the "JVM<->Node protocol kept separable (no one complete string baked into every layer)" deliverable of rf2-hic-056 (garbage-collected; text in checkpoint `09a7e2dcf7:.beads/issues.jsonl`), and, for the module contract, the design-lane clause at `docs/design/fresco/product/lanes/react-compatibility-notes.md:106` and "Streaming stays behind the server abstraction" at `docs/design/fresco/product/specification.md:307`. Those design documents are records and stay unedited. ## Work All in `implementation/ssr-node` plus the module's consumers. **No JVM source change**: nothing under `implementation/ssr-ring/src` or `implementation/ssr/src` moves, because the JVM never used streaming or read `x-rf-ssr-chunks`. - `src/worker.cjs`: delete `emit` and the chunk posting (`:170-184`) and the return-value refusal (`:240-257`). Await `module.render(call)`; a string is the body; anything else is the closed `render-threw` refusal that names the returned value's type tag and never its content. The worker still builds the completion record (render duration and the rest) from its own clocks, so nothing module-supplied crosses except the HTML string. - `src/isolate.cjs`: delete `stampAfterChunks` and its torn-response commentary (`:75-100`). The per-chunk `onChunk` callback (`:256`) becomes one result. - `src/service.cjs`: delete the `renderFrames` async generator (`:102-202`) and `pendingFrames`; the one render call returns the body (`renderToString` at `:208-216` today joins the frames). - `src/http.cjs`: delete `?stream=1` (`:187-232`), surrogate hold-back (`:124-140`), the torn-response path and `x-rf-ssr-chunks` (`:241`). The buffered 200 keeps `x-rf-ssr-build`, `x-rf-ssr-render-ms` and `x-rf-ssr-request`. - `src/protocol.cjs`: delete `MODULE_RETURN_REFUSAL` (`:207-212`, export at `:716`), the `emit`-only output-channel commentary (around `:87`), and the chunk-frame and `afterChunks` shapes. - `src/envelope.cjs`: reword the bounded quantity from "to the last frame of its response being delivered" (`:15-16`) to "to its response being delivered". Move the file to `test/` with `git mv`, so `git log --follow` keeps the pre-registration witness its header cites; `package.json` `exports` does not ship it. The move is housekeeping, not a prerequisite. Keep `test/envelope.test.cjs` (the witness at `:63`) and its ceilings unchanged; it measures service overhead, not total render or JVM/HTTP latency. - Tests: `test/bytes.test.cjs`, `test/egress.test.cjs`, `test/protocol.test.cjs`, `test/timeout.test.cjs`, `test/_support.cjs`, and the envelope test's require path. Every fixture under `test/fixtures/` returns a string. Delete `chunked.cjs`. Repurpose `null-return.cjs` (or replace it) as the non-string-return refusal fixture. - JVM-side Node fixtures: `implementation/ssr-ring/test/fixtures/node/crossing.cjs` and `login_host.cjs` return strings. - Fresco CLJS witness `implementation/fresco/test/re_frame/fresco/login_server_crossing_ssr_dom_cljs_test.cljs`: `hand-to-module!` (`:205-215`) and the `(undefined? returned)` assertion (`:299-300`) move to the string contract. - Taught module `examples/substrates/fresco/login/server.cljs`: `render!` returns `render-body`'s string; the `emit` / `js/undefined` docstring (`:46`) and the trailing `js/undefined` (`:114`, `:140`) go. - `implementation/ssr-node/README.md`: guarantee 5 (table row `:41`, section `:207-235`) gets the "response delivered" wording; "The protocol, and why it is kept separable" (`:266`), "Response frames" (`:359`) and "The render module contract" (`:450-612`) describe one buffered output and drop `?stream=1`. - `docs/ssr/concepts.md` §Render on Node, step 2 (`:780-871`): the code sample loses `emit` and `js/undefined`, and the "`render` returns `js/undefined`, not `nil`" paragraph (`:863-866`) goes. - `CHANGELOG.md` `[Unreleased]`: one entry announcing the pre-alpha render-module contract change. The package is `private: true`, but checkout-based users may exist. Deliberately stays: - `renderToString` in Fresco's `render-body`. Neither the sidecar nor the JVM escapes the finished HTML again; the body bytes pass through unchanged. - The request field list and `protocol: 1`. This is pre-alpha, so revise in place with no compatibility layer. - `:args`, the fixed public error wording, the answer-side build check (`node.clj:428`), immutable snapshots (structured clone + freeze), admission bounds, hard termination and isolate replacement, and service-owned response and error metadata. - `spec/011-SSR.md` needs no change: it never describes the module's output channel. If a worker does touch it, note that it is the one `i/crlf` file in the repo. ## Sequencing - Hot zones touched: **none**. - Depends on: no bead. The allowlist-retirement bead filed alongside this one (ssr-node: retire the per-entry stateAllowlist/runtimeAllowlist) comes after this one, because both edit `protocol.cjs`, `worker.cjs`, the README, the fixtures, the login `server.cljs` and `docs/ssr/concepts.md`. One worker can take both as two commits. - Cross-dossier: `docs/ssr/concepts.md` is shared with the work from `ssr-server-init-reserved-name.md` and `ssr-mismatch-detection-hash-channels.md`. Those touch other sections, but sequence the PRs. If `ssr-mismatch-detection-hash-channels.md` rules that the `:renderer` seam returns the body alone, that changes `node.clj` and not the Node module contract here; no ordering is required, but the two must not run in parallel on `node.clj` docstrings. - Gates: `npm run test:ssr-node --prefix implementation` (plain Node, outside the shadow-cljs lane); the ssr-ring `:crossing-test` alias (CI job `jvm-node-crossing`); the Fresco CLJS witness and the login server compile, which enter shadow-cljs (run only under a coordinator grant, or cite CI); `mkdocs build --strict` plus `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` for `docs/ssr/concepts.md`; and `scripts/check_readme_links.py --ci` for the ssr-node README and `CHANGELOG.md`. ## Evidence Read in source at trunk 89517e8f54: every `path:line` above, the `MODULE_RETURN_REFUSAL` text, the `emit` closure, `renderFrames` and `pendingFrames`, the `?stream=1` branch, the JVM `/render` URI and its buffered return, `render-body` returning `renderToString`'s HTML, and `package.json` (`private: true`, `exports` without the envelope). Codex ran a read-only probe against the installed React/ReactDOM 19.3.0: `renderToString` gives `
ab
` where `renderToStaticMarkup` gives `
ab
`, ordinary text is escaped, and `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` passes through raw. Still needs a run, because nothing was executed: login body-byte invariance through the real crossing, the timeout, replacement and build-skew paths, and the line-count estimates (about 300 streaming source lines removed, size S-M).
acceptance_criteria:
1. The render module contract is `render(call) -> string | Promise<string>`. A search of `implementation/`, `examples/` and `docs/ssr/` for `MODULE_RETURN_REFUSAL`, `renderFrames`, `pendingFrames`, `afterChunks`, `x-rf-ssr-chunks`, `stream=1` and the module's `emit` parameter finds nothing.
2. A module returning a non-string (`undefined`, `null`, a number, an object, or a promise resolving to one of those) is refused with `:rf.ssr-node/render-threw` and the closed wording. The refusal carries at most the returned value's type tag, and no module-supplied text reaches the wire (an egress test asserts this).
3. Through the real JVM -> Node -> JVM crossing, the login example's body bytes are unchanged against trunk, and neither the sidecar nor the JVM re-escapes the HTML. Fresco's `render-body` still uses `renderToString`.
4. Hard termination on timeout, isolate replacement, and the build-identity-mismatch refusal behave as before (ssr-node timeout and serve tests, and the crossing build-mismatch arm).
5. `test/envelope.test.cjs` still runs with unchanged ceilings, and the envelope's wording bounds the time "to its response being delivered", not to a last frame.
6. `git diff` shows no change under `implementation/ssr-ring/src/` or `implementation/ssr/src/`.
7. The login `server.cljs` and the CLJS witness `login_server_crossing_ssr_dom_cljs_test.cljs` use the string return. `docs/ssr/concepts.md` step 2 teaches it with no `js/undefined` rule. The ssr-node README's module-contract and protocol sections describe one buffered output. `CHANGELOG.md` `[Unreleased]` records the contract change.
8. Green, with the exit codes quoted in the PR: `npm run test:ssr-node --prefix implementation`; the ssr-ring `:crossing-test` alias (or CI `jvm-node-crossing`); the Fresco CLJS witness (locally under a coordinator grant, or CI); `mkdocs build --strict`; `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py`; and `scripts/check_readme_links.py --ci`.
notes:
== WORKER NOTE 2026-10-16 (PR #11367, branch worker/ssr-node-string-body, base ba10ed2e72)

Implemented as ruled. render(call) -> string | Promise<string>; the worker posts one complete message {html, renderMs} and the service's one call is renderToString(), resolving with COMPLETE_FIELDS = type, html, renderMs, buildId, requestId. Deleted: emit and chunk posting, MODULE_RETURN_REFUSAL and the exact-undefined rule, stampAfterChunks and every afterChunks field, renderFrames/pendingFrames, chunkFrame, ?stream=1, surrogate hold-back, the torn-response socket destroy, x-rf-ssr-chunks. envelope.cjs moved to test/ by git mv (git log --follow still reaches the pre-registration commit f39829caa6); its bounded quantity now ends at "its response being delivered"; ceilings unchanged. chunked.cjs deleted; null-return.cjs became non-string-return.cjs (undefined, null, number, object, promise-of-null, promise-of-object refused; string and promise-of-string as the control). No change under implementation/ssr-ring/src or implementation/ssr/src.

One reading to flag: the ruling says a non-string is refused "with the existing closed render-threw wording". RENDER_THREW_REFUSAL's text says "the render module threw" and points the operator at a stderr exception that does not exist for a bad return, so the refusal uses the render-threw code with a fixed contract-owned message instead ("the render module returned no body markup: `render` must return a string, or a promise of one") and detail {entry, returned: <type tag>}. Evidence: npm run test:ssr-node exit 0, 74 tests (baseline at tip 79: -1 streaming-destroy egress row, -1 torn-timeout row, -3 streaming/chunk bytes rows; every count matched its prediction). title: docs(http): Spec 009, the http API doc and two Xray comments still describe the pre-one-record managed-HTTP internals
description:
rf2-84xkm (PR #11365) rebuilt the managed-HTTP lifecycle as one request record in one registry, changed only through `send!`, `completed!`, `fire!` and `abort!`, with one retire site inside `commit!`. Its worker reported prose outside its fence that still describes the old internals. The behaviour each line describes is checked against the merged code, not this list.

- `spec/009-Instrumentation.md` ~2276: says aborts are also re-labelled after a completion wins the race. That no longer happens.
- `spec/009-Instrumentation.md` ~2322: says a retry "mints a fresh handle that bypasses the once-only reply guard". There is no separate handle now; the retry is a transition of the one record.
- `docs/api/re-frame.http.md` ~528: says "both indexes". There is one registry.
- `tools/xray/src/**/managed_fx_helpers.cljc` ~301 and ~723: comments name the deleted functions. The behaviour they describe still holds; rename to the current transition names.

Line numbers are from the worker's report against its branch; re-derive at tip.

Hot zone: `spec/009-Instrumentation.md`. Sequential with any other 009 holder; rf2-qpyus is the natural cluster partner (also 009 prose only).

description: At PR #11374 merged SHA 4a0e9c9a3b312d92cc31ca466c05c854da177ca8, spec/012-Routing.md:843 expands the raw-URL validation row to all three doors but still says no :rf.error/*, no trace and no always-on report; line 845 says only the not-found view exposes this failure in a release build. title: Conformance spec: state how :fixture/spec-version is compared (harness claims a version set; unclaimed fixtures skip, never fail)
description:
The conformance spec says that fixtures carry `:fixture/spec-version`, but not what a port declares or how the two are compared. A port therefore can't reach the reference harness's behaviour from the spec alone. This is spec gap G6, found by the spec-only port probe rf2-9bh05.

## Ruling

`:fixture/spec-version` stays: there is no mass edit and no removal. This was settled on 2026-10-16. Both reviews of the conformance dossier agreed on everything else, and Codex's position on this one detail was adopted under Mike's direction: "file necessary beads for the "Largely in agreement" list as outlined above". This bead replaces rf2-09wtw, which was held only on that question.

## Evidence (trunk 818479f34b)

- `spec/conformance/README.md:403-411` (§Versioning) shows a fixture declaring `:fixture/spec-version "1.0"`. It says the corpus is versioned alongside the spec, and nothing more about how the key is used.
- The probe's gap-log entry G6 quotes the README as claiming "the corpus's harness check rejects implementations that haven't moved with the spec". The README never says what a port declares, where it declares it, or how the comparison works. The probe ignored the key, which had no effect on pass/fail.
- The reference harness does compare:
  - `implementation/core/test/re_frame/conformance_runner.cljc:199-202` holds `claimed-spec-versions`, the set of versions the implementation claims.
  - `spec-version-claimed?` (`:239-245`) treats a fixture with no `:fixture/spec-version` as unversioned, so it runs. Otherwise the fixture runs only if its version is in the claimed set.
  - A fixture whose version is not in the set is reported as SKIPPED with reason "spec-version not in claimed set" (`:1761-1765`), not failed.

## Change

Write the rule into §Versioning of `spec/conformance/README.md`. If the grammar file carries the key, add a line to its description in `spec/conformance/fixture-file.edn`. The rule has four parts:
- a harness declares the set of spec versions it claims;
- a fixture whose `:fixture/spec-version` is in that set runs;
- a fixture with no version runs as unversioned;
- any other fixture is reported as skipped with its version, never failed.

Correct the "rejects implementations" wording if it overstates this, because the harness skips; it does not reject. Do not change runtime behaviour or touch the fixtures.

Gates: `mkdocs build --strict` and `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py`. If `fixture-file.edn` changes, also run `re-frame.conformance-grammar-test`. No hot-zone files.
acceptance_criteria:
1. §Versioning of `spec/conformance/README.md` states all four parts of the rule: what a harness declares, that a claimed version runs, that an unversioned fixture runs, and that an unclaimed version is reported as skipped with its version and never failed. Each part matches `conformance_runner.cljc`.
2. No sentence claims the harness "rejects" an implementation for its version.
3. No fixture or runner code changes. `mkdocs build --strict` and `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` exit 0.

title: Remove retired hash-tier and second-serialiser guidance from Spec 011
description:
Audit of PR #11467 at e64c55fa7265994256cec14408e45b4626235460. Spec 011's live emitter rationale still describes the retired second serialiser and render-tree hash channel:
- spec/011-SSR.md:283 says the render-tree hash compares the tree even when HTML differs.
- :285 calls the hiccup path the hash tier, says a leading-LF text divergence escapes that tier, and contrasts it with React adoption; it also describes both SSR serialisers and the removed structural serialiser's wider input.
- :287 still justifies the roster by two SSR serialisers.

This contradicts the same spec's current Hydration-mismatch detection contract at :672: every React-family root, including Reagent, reports recoveries through React adoption alone, nothing else compares output, and the payload carries state rather than a page fingerprint. The source bead's predecessor hash-channel retirement and this PR's removal of emit-ui-tree deliberately leave one hiccup serialiser. The helper move itself is correct: read-form comparison, normalizing regex pattern/flags and ignoring docstrings, found all four moved definitions equal and no changed pre-existing helper body. No runtime defect was found.

Small correction: restate these three rationale paragraphs for the single hiccup emitter and React adoption. Keep the real ARIA/boolean distinction, leading-LF compensation, attribute-only reporting limit, and independent react-dom evidence. Remove only the dead second-serialiser/hash-tier explanations; no new hash mechanism or runtime guard is needed. Use the documented docs gates and manual prose reading.

The complete closed source rf2-9kbu2 was read; its close reason/notes record these outside-fence remnants. This new open bead preserves a separately trackable audit correction, linked to that source with only an appended forward pointer.

Both ~283 and ~285 cited a sub-heading, "What React-native adoption does not catch", that Hydration-mismatch detection no longer has. Its boundary paragraph is now titled "The boundary".

Done, in spec/011-SSR.md only:
- ~283: the attribute-only divergence escapes because React adoption, the only check that compares server and client output, neither patches nor reports it. This cites "The boundary". The render-tree hash sentence is gone.
- ~285: the "case for stating the rule once ... render-tree hash" sentence is gone, along with the hash-tier, adoption-tier and "both channels" contrast. The parallel with the boolean paragraph is now the shared authority, not what catches a miss. A lone string child left uncompensated is a text mismatch that React recovers from and reports, as :rf.ssr/hydration-mismatch plus a client re-render of that subtree, so the fix stays in the emitter. The source for this is react-dom 19.3.0's prepareToHydrateHostInstance, which calls throwOnHydrationMismatch when string children disagree with textContent. title: ssr-node: rewrite the README present-tense without its Provenance section, and correct the worker header's isolation claim
description:
## Current

- Do not change how the sidecar is packaged or installed; that choice is held for Mike on rf2-8arzr.8.

- Every guarantee it lists has a witness test.
- `scripts/check_readme_links.py --ci` stays green.

title: capture-frame docstring: state the lifetime rule (a live capture pins its incarnation; an absent id follows the address)
description:
## Current

Spec 002 (~1528) gives the lifetime rule for `capture-frame`. Capturing a live frame id pins that incarnation, so the captured ops go inert once it is destroyed. Capturing an absent id pins nothing, and the ops follow whoever holds the id when they run.

The public docstring of `capture-frame` (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/core.cljc` ~1416) talks only about the id.

## Change

Add those two sentences to the docstring. No new verb, no warning and no behaviour change. Rejecting absent ids is not wanted, because following an address is an intentional capability.

## Acceptance

The docstring states both cases in the present tense and matches Spec 002's rule.

Checked at trunk f4e5adad0a.
notes:
== DONE (worker core-internals, 2026-10-19, PR #11504, branch worker/core-internals) ==

Premise held at tip 560f3b2829. Spec 002 line 1528 states the lifetime rule, and the code agrees with it: re-frame.capture-frame/capture-target-incarnation pins a live id's incarnation and pins nothing for an absent id. The capture-frame docstring in core.cljc spoke only of the id.

Change: the docstring gains one present-tense paragraph, placed before the "A per-call :frame" paragraph. It says the frame api is pinned to the incarnation live at capture, not merely to its id. Once that incarnation is destroyed, the dispatch ops do nothing and :subscribe returns nil, each emitting :rf.error/frame-destroyed, even after a new frame is created under the same id. Capturing an id with no live frame pins nothing, and its ops follow whichever frame holds the id when they run. No new verb, no warning and no behaviour change.

title: :dispatch-later takes an optional :id that replaces or cancels a pending timer (debounce without a library)
description:
## Problem

Measured at trunk 3959d2a5bf.

Each `:dispatch-later` arms an anonymous host timer: `implementation/core/src/re_frame/fx.cljc` § `:dispatch-later` host-timer side table keys every pending timer by a monotonic counter, and only `destroy-frame!` cancels one. So three common needs have no direct spelling: debounce (search as you type), replace a pending dispatch, and cancel one when the user leaves. Today they need either a machine state with `:after` (re-entering the state re-arms its timer) or app code holding host handles outside the pipeline.

## Against

`spec/Principles.md` § The demand bar warns against "a second run-this-later surface, a third debounce mechanism", and a public `:rf.timer/after` surface is deliberately deferred (`spec/Managed-Effects.md`, the paragraph on the test-only `re-frame.timer-probe`; EP-0011). This bead adds **no new surface**: it is an optional key on the existing `:dispatch-later`, which `spec/Principles.md`'s fixed-and-additive rule governs. A machine's `:after` stays the tool when a timer belongs to a state's lifecycle.

## Change

- `:dispatch-later` accepts an optional `:id`, any EDN value, scoped to the frame.
- Arming with an `:id` that is still pending cancels the pending timer first, so the later call replaces it. This is debounce.
- A cancel spelling on the same fx, for example `{:id k :cancel? true}`. Settle the spelling against the fx's argument schema.
- An ordinary trace (not a warning) when a pending timer is replaced or cancelled, so Xray can show it.
- Frame destroy still cancels everything. The table stays a transient host cache: never in runtime-db, never on the SSR, hydration or epoch wire.

**Named consumer.** Write one debounced-search recipe in the docs with `:id`, beside the same behaviour written as a machine with `:after`. If the machine form is as short and as clear, close this bead with the comparison recorded and change nothing.

## Spec and docs that move with it

- `spec/002-Frames.md`, the `:dispatch-later` rows and the frame-teardown list. **Hot zone.**
- The `:dispatch-later` fx row in `spec/API.md` with both manifest sidecars, and the reserved-fx row in `spec/Conventions.md`. **Hot zones.**
- A trace row in `spec/009-Instrumentation.md`, if a trace id is added. **Hot zone.**

## Acceptance

- Two arms with the same `:id` inside the delay produce one dispatch, of the later event.
- A cancel produces none.
- The same `:id` in two frames is independent.
- Frame destroy clears pending id'd timers.
- An arm without `:id` behaves exactly as today.
- JVM suite and `npm run test:cljs` green.

## Sequencing

Hot zones: `spec/002-Frames.md`, `spec/API.md` with its sidecars, `spec/Conventions.md`, possibly `spec/009-Instrumentation.md`.

Additive. Effort S–M.
notes:
== WORKER SUMMARY (PR #11534, branch worker/core-dispatch-later-errors, 2026-10-19 AUSEST)

Disposition: DONE. Not closed here; the mayor closes on merge.

Named-consumer comparison (the bead's gate on whether to change anything): the debounced search written with :id is one key on the :dispatch-later the input handler already returns. The same behaviour as a machine needs a reg-machine (an :idle/:waiting pair, a :reenter? true self-transition on :typed, an :after 250 transition carrying a :settle action that dispatches the settle event), a snapshot in the frame, and a second event per keystroke to reach it. The machine form is not as short or as clear, so the change went ahead. Both forms are written side by side in docs/core/effects.md, section "Debounce: give the timer an :id".

What changed:
- implementation/core/src/re_frame/fx.cljc: :dispatch-later accepts an optional :id (any value, frame-scoped). Arming a pending :id removes and cancels it in the same atomic swap that reserves the new slot. The slot key still carries a fresh counter value beside the :id, so a replaced timer's already-started callback finds its own slot gone and dispatches nothing. {:id k :cancel? true} cancels the pending timer and arms nothing; a cancel without :id raises :rf.error/fx-handler-exception (same channel as a bad :ms). Each replace or cancel of a pending timer emits the ordinary dev trace :rf.fx/dispatch-later-cancelled, op-type :rf.fx, tags {:frame :id :reason :on-replace|:on-cancel}. Frame destroy and the test-isolation reset still cancel every pending timer, id'd or not. The name lives only in the transient host table.
- Spec: 002 (paragraph "Naming a :dispatch-later timer" under :fx ordering and atomicity guarantees), Spec-Schemas DispatchLaterFxArgs (now an :or of the arm map with optional :id and the cancel map), Conventions reserved-fx row and the :rf.fx/* row, 009 quick-reference row and detailed bullet for :rf.fx/dispatch-later-cancelled.
- Docs: docs/core/effects.md debounce section (with the machine comparison), docs/api/re-frame.core.md :dispatch-later entry, docs/core/fresco/08-async-resources.md search recipe now debounces with :id and cancels on clear (its generation guard is gone), skills fx reference row.

Held for the mayor (hot zone not held by this worker): spec/API.md's Standard :fx entries row for :dispatch-later. Exact row:
| `[:dispatch-later {:ms ms :event event-vec}]` | options map | v1 | 002 | An optional `:id` names the timer within the frame: re-arming it replaces the pending timer, and `{:id id :cancel? true}` cancels it (per [002 §`:fx` ordering and atomicity guarantees](002-Frames.md#fx-ordering-and-atomicity-guarantees)). |

Evidence: implementation/core/test/re_frame/dispatch_later_id_test.clj, 7 tests. At trunk 3959d2a5bf, 3 of them failed (replace, cancel, trace); all 7 pass with the change, as do the existing dispatch-later-frame-destroy and bad-ms namespaces (14 tests, 21 assertions, exit 0). The trace test is ^:requires-debug and the rest pass under the prod-gate lane.

Merged in PR #11534 (squash, commit 0dac4b4476). :dispatch-later takes an optional, frame-scoped :id.
- Re-arming the same :id replaces the pending timer.
- {:id k :cancel? true} cancels it. A cancel without :id is refused with :rf.error/fx-handler-exception.
- Each replace or cancel emits :rf.fx/dispatch-later-cancelled, with :reason :on-replace or :on-cancel.
- destroy-frame! still cancels every pending timer.

The machine-form comparison the bead asked for is in docs/core/effects.md: one key on the handler's existing :dispatch-later, against a reg-machine with a :reenter? self-transition and an :after. The Fresco search recipe now uses :id.

title: Emit singleton completion when bootstrap enters finality
description:
Merged PR #11538, f3565f964881f2b8b706c27bb97aafa8af0c3970. A valid singleton whose initial state is already final never emits :rf.machine/done. The same occurs when a parallel singleton starts with every region final and no root :on-done. registration.cljc:828-829 defines entered-finality? by comparing next-snapshot with ctx.snapshot, but prepare-machine-ctx has already seeded the latter with the final initial configuration before its first bootstrap. The comparison therefore treats birth as an already-resting machine and skips rest-machine, including its completion-output validation. This misses the one completion promised for entry into whole-machine finality.

Evidence: focused JVM probe ai/pr-audit/pr-audit-sol-oct11-11538-initial-final-1.clj (log and exit alongside it; exit 0). All 34 owning machines source files matched the merge blobs. Through real reg-machine, dispatch-sync and trace capture, the ordinary idle -> done control emitted one done trace. A flat :initial :done singleton and a parallel singleton with two initially final regions both remained readable but emitted zero; a later poke was silent too. Existing final_singleton_rest_test covers transition into finality, not finality at bootstrap.

Small correction: make a successful bootstrap into finality count as entry, using the existing bootstrap/liveness context rather than only the seeded state comparison. Preserve the resting no-op suppression. Cover flat and parallel initially-final singletons: one done on birth, none on later unhandled events, and completion-output validation still runs.
notes:
== DISPATCH (mayor), 2026-10-19 21:27:46 AUSEST: worker machines-bootstrap-final (branch worker/machines-bootstrap-final). It owns lifecycle_fx/registration.cljc at the finality-entry code only, plus final_singleton_rest_test.clj or a new test beside it.
== WORKER (machines-bootstrap-final), 2026-10-19 22:15 AUSEST: DONE in PR #11548 (commits 015b7d1924, 02b5a3f489, d202cdeb34).

Both birth routes were wrong. LAZY (first real event): commit-or-finalize compared the post-step snapshot with ctx :snapshot, which prepare-machine-ctx had already seeded with the final initial configuration, so birth read as resting and skipped rest-machine and its completion-output validation. EAGER ([:rf.machine/start]): the pure init-kick branch sent every final birth to finalize-machine, singletons included, so a born-final singleton was torn down. Its next event re-births it, so fixing only the lazy route would have produced a second completion.

Fix (registration.cljc, finality-entry code only): entered-finality? is finished? AND (needs-bootstrap? OR a pre-step snapshot that was not final). The start-marker branch routes a booted final snapshot through the existing whole-machine-final?: a spawned actor to finalize-machine, a singleton to rest-machine. That branch is gated on :needs-bootstrap?, so a redundant start on an already-booted machine is no entry and commits unchanged. Resting no-op suppression is unchanged. There is no new vocabulary.

Evidence: final_singleton_rest_test.clj gains three tests, each over a flat :initial :done singleton and a parallel singleton with two initially-final regions: lazy birth gives one done and none on a later unhandled event; eager start gives one done, none on a later event or a redundant start, and the singleton rests unreaped; a [:schemas :output] violation at birth emits the :where :machine-output :phase :completion trace and still completes. At trunk source: 8 tests, 29 assertions, 14 failures (exit 1). With the fix: 0 failures (exit 0).

Machines JVM lane: 667 tests, 1586 assertions, 0 failures (exit 0). That is +3 tests and +20 assertions over #11538's 664/1566, as predicted. Fast-PR spine exit 0: core JVM 1195/3603, test:cljs 6197/17502. CI green: 80 checks, 63 success, 17 skipped.

Outside the fence: birth_always_cljs_test.cljc's eager-start-onto-final test asserted the pre-D7 teardown (nil snapshot). It was the only red in the machines lane and now asserts that the singleton rests. No live worker held that file.

Held for the mayor: spec/005 § The start marker callout still says a final eager birth "runs the :on-done + auto-destroy cascade exactly as the lazy path would". The replacement sentence (spawned actor reaped, singleton rests with its one :rf.machine/done) is in the PR body.
== MERGED CODE (mayor), 2026-10-19 22:11:36 AUSEST: PR #11548 rebase-merged at 1c21fe6764. Birth into finality now counts as entry on both routes: the lazy route (entered-finality? is true when bootstrapped) and the eager route ([:rf.machine/start] sends a final birth through whole-machine-final?, so a spawned actor is finalized and a singleton rests). Three new tests are in final_singleton_rest_test.clj: they went red at trunk (14 failures) and pass with the fix. The machines JVM lane passed with 667 tests and 1586 assertions. CI was green: 80 checks, 63 passed, 17 skipped. birth_always_cljs_test.cljc's eager-start-onto-final pin was updated to the D7 rest; the mayor accepted that fence crossing.
== FENCE (mayor), 2026-10-19 22:11:36 AUSEST: OPEN until spec/005 § The start marker's pure-init-kick sentence is changed so a final eager birth rests a singleton, as the lazy path does. Released to the same worker on branch worker/spec005-born-final. CLEARS WHEN that PR merges; close this bead then.
close_reason:
Merged in two PRs.

Code: PR #11548 (rebase, merge 1c21fe6764). Birth into whole-machine finality now counts as entry on both routes. On the lazy route (first real event), entered-finality? is true when this call bootstrapped the machine, not only when the seeded snapshot changed. On the eager route ([:rf.machine/start]), a final birth goes through whole-machine-final?: a spawned actor goes to finalize-machine and a singleton to rest-machine, gated on :needs-bootstrap? so a redundant start commits unchanged. Resting no-op suppression is unchanged. birth_always_cljs_test.cljc's pre-D7 teardown pin now asserts the rest.

CI was green on #11548 (80 checks) and #11550 (79 checks).

title: Schemas: an app-db validation-failure trace ignores the frame's elision registry, so a registry-classified sensitive path leaks
description:
## Problem

Measured at trunk 8fc6369484 (found while removing a flow's own :schema under rf2-7wokd).

An `:rf.error/schema-validation-failure` trace with `:where :app-db` decides redaction from the schema's own `:sensitive?` props only. `validate-app-schema!` (`implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/validate.cljc`) never consults the frame's elision registry.

So a path classified sensitive by the registry, rather than by the schema, ships its value in the failure trace. Measured: a flow `{:inputs [[:secret]] :output-path [:auth :token] :sensitive [[]]}` writing `{:token "hunter2-SECRET"}`, with `(rf/reg-app-schema [:auth :token] [:map [:token :int]])`. One failure trace reaches a plain trace listener, and its `pr-str` contains "hunter2-SECRET".

The same holds for any registry classification at a schema'd path: commit-plane `:sensitive` effects, and machine, route or resource declarations.

The removed flow-output arm did consult the registry. Its `:value` went through `rf.elision/elide-wire-value`, and its `:explain` was redacted whole when the registry classified the output. With rf2-7wokd, `reg-app-schema` is the only way to declare a flow's output shape, so this gap now covers that case too.

## Question

Should the `:app-db` arm project `:value` / `:explain` through the frame's elision registry, as `:rf.sub/run` and `:rf.flow/computed` do at emit? Or is the schema's `:sensitive?` prop the intended single source for validation traces? In that case the docs should tell authors to mark the schema slot as well.

The workaround today is to mark the slot `{:sensitive? true}` in the app schema.
notes:
== RULING (mayor, under the project stance), 2026-10-20 09:31:15 AUSEST: the :app-db arm of :rf.error/schema-validation-failure projects :value and :explain through the frame elision registry, as :rf.sub/run and :rf.flow/computed do at emit. :explain is redacted whole when the registry classifies the path, as the removed flow-output arm did. The schema :sensitive? prop stays as an additional way to mark a slot. Why: the registry is the one classification, so authors never declare a path sensitive twice (the same declare-once principle as the rf2-7wokd ruling), and fail-closed is the safe direction. Mike may overrule.
== DISPATCH (mayor), 2026-10-20 09:31:15 AUSEST: added to the schemas-sub-flow-recovery cluster (worker that found it; PR #11561, draft; holder of spec/009 and spec/010). Scope: validate-app-schema! in implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/validate.cljc and its tests.
== WORKER (schemas-sub-flow-recovery), 2026-10-20 10:20 AUSEST: implemented per the mayor's ruling on PR #11561, commit 895f41d09c.
- validate-app-schema! (implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/validate.cljc) projects each :app-db failure through the frame's elision registry AFTER the schema-driven redaction (new private project-through-registry):
  - :value, narrowed to the failing leaf, is walked by rf.elision/elide-wire-value at the leaf's own path. A slot the schema already redacted or size-elided is left alone.
  - :explain / :explain-humanized (whole registered value) are redacted whole with :sensitive? true when the registry classifies anything in the registered value sensitive. Otherwise they are replaced by a size marker (:large? true) when it classifies anything there large.
  - The walk reads the frame's LIVE registry, as the removed flow-output arm and the :rf.flow/computed emit do. So a commit-plane classification effect returned by the SAME event that writes the failing value is not yet in it. The flow's own output marks are claimed before evaluation, so they are.
- Tests (schemas_sensitive_test.clj), red at trunk with 6 failures, green after:
  - app-db-validation-redacts-a-registry-sensitive-path covers a commit-plane :sensitive effect and a flow's own :sensitive [[]] output (the measured case).
  - app-db-validation-size-elides-a-registry-large-path covers a commit-plane :large effect.
  - Schemas suite: 131 tests / 412 assertions, exit 0 (was 129 / 406).
- Spec 010 §:sensitive? (the "per-slot schema props only" sentence) and Spec 009's classification note now say the app-db arm reads the registry too.
Merged-PR audit #11561: follow-up rf2-skx61 — Schemas: redact failures with the same event's classification effects. This is a separate open finding; the source status and ruling are preserved.
close_reason:
Merged in PR #11561 (squash, 2026-10-20T01:24:56Z; trunk 07250ba2b0). Ruled under the posture: one classification, declared once.
- An :rf.error/schema-validation-failure trace with :where :app-db now projects through the frame's elision registry. :value is walked at the leaf path. :explain is redacted whole when sensitive, or size-marked when large.
- The schema :sensitive? prop stays as an additional way to mark.
- Tests in schemas_sensitive_test.clj (commit-plane :sensitive, a flow's own :sensitive [[]] output, commit-plane :large) went red at trunk first (6 failures). The schemas suite is now 131 tests / 412 assertions.
- Two security precision tests moved onto a live frame, because the walker fails closed on an unresolvable frame.
- RESIDUAL, filed as rf2-a46kl: the walk reads the LIVE registry, so a classification effect returned by the same event is not yet covered.
